title: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.3 Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation
intro: After this lesson you can define random process, outcome and event, explain probability as long-run relative frequency, state the law of large numbers, and design and carry out a simulation to estimate a probability.

moments.title: Random process
moments.text: A process whose results are determined by chance. You know the possible outcomes but not which will occur.

moments.title: Outcome and event
moments.text: An outcome is the result of one trial. An event is a collection of outcomes, such as an odd number on a die.

moments.title: Probability
moments.text: The long-run relative frequency of an outcome or event over a large number of trials.

moments.title: Simulation
moments.text: A model of a random process that uses chance numbers in place of the real trials.

moments.title: At least three heads in five tosses
moments.text: Let 1 be a head and 2 a tail. Generate five numbers per trial and count the ones.

moments.title: Five simulation steps
moments.text: Assign numbers, generate them, count what you need, define a success, then repeat many trials.

moments.title: Repeats allowed for independent trials
moments.text: Coin tosses do not remember each other, so the same number may appear again.

moments.title: Estimate from trials
moments.text: Estimated probability is the number of successful trials divided by the number of trials.

moments.title: Law of large numbers
moments.text: For independent trials, the long-run relative frequency gets closer and closer to a single value as trials increase.

moments.title: Eight stores chosen from 800
moments.text: Numbers 001 to 500 are US stores, 501 to 800 are European. Pick eight with no repeats and count US numbers.

moments.title: No repeats when sampling without replacement
moments.text: A store cannot be chosen twice, so the simulation must not repeat a number in one trial.

moments.title: A 72% free-throw shooter
moments.text: Use 00 to 71 for a make and 72 to 99 for a miss. Generate ten numbers per trial and count makes.

moments.title: Match the number range to the probability
moments.text: A 72% chance needs 72 of 100 two-digit numbers assigned to a make.

moments.title: Five parts of a simulation design
moments.text: Say which numbers are used, whether repeats are allowed, how many to pick, what to count, and what is a success.

sections.title: Can numbers repeat in one trial?

cards.name: Repeats allowed
cards.text: Each selection is independent, like a coin toss or a free throw.

cards.name: No repeats
cards.text: Items are chosen from a fixed group and cannot be chosen twice.

cells: A store cannot be chosen twice.
Choose 3 students from a class of 20 for a team
The same student cannot be chosen twice.
Draw 5 cards from a deck without replacement
A card cannot be drawn twice.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Ask whether the same person, item or number could occur twice in a real trial. If not, turn repeats off.

questions.obj: Design a simulation for five coin tosses
questions.q: Design a simulation to estimate the probability that at least three of five tosses of a fair coin are heads.

steps.t: Assign numbers to the outcomes so their proportions match the probabilities.

work.text: Two numbers for two equally likely outcomes. Any two numbers would do.

steps.t: Say how many numbers to generate per trial and whether repeats are allowed.

work.text: Generate 5 numbers from 1 to 2 for each trial. Repeats are allowed because each toss is independent of the others.

steps.t: Say what to count in each trial.

work.text: Count how many of the 5 numbers are 1s, because a 1 represents a head.
At least three heads means three, four, or five heads.

steps.t: Repeat for many trials, then estimate the probability.

work.text: Many trials are needed because the true probability only shows itself in the long run. A handful of trials, such as 2 successes in 7, is not enough.

questions.answer: Let 1 be a head and 2 a tail. Generate 5 numbers from 1 to 2 with repeats allowed. Count the 1s. A trial is a success if there are at least three 1s. Repeat for many trials and divide the number of successes by the number of trials to estimate the probability.

questions.obj: Design a simulation without repeats for eight stores
questions.q: A company has 800 stores: 500 in the US and 300 in Europe. Eight stores are chosen at random. Design a simulation to estimate the probability that all eight are in the US.

steps.t: Assign numbers to the outcomes so their proportions match the probabilities.

work.text: Each store gets its own number. 500 of the 800 numbers represent US stores.

steps.t: Say how many numbers to generate per trial and whether repeats are allowed.

work.text: Generate 8 different numbers from 1 to 800 for each trial. Repeats are not allowed because a store cannot be chosen twice.

steps.t: Say what to count in each trial.

work.text: Count how many of the 8 numbers are from 001 to 500.
All eight stores must be in the US, so all eight numbers must be 500 or less.

steps.t: Repeat for many trials, then estimate the probability.

work.text: Ten trials with no successes would not show that the probability is 0. Run many more trials.

questions.answer: Let 001 to 500 be the US stores and 501 to 800 the European stores. Generate 8 different numbers from 1 to 800 with no repeats. Count the numbers from 001 to 500. A trial is a success if all 8 are from 001 to 500. Repeat for many trials and divide the number of successes by the number of trials.

questions.obj: Design a simulation for a percentage-based probability
questions.q: McKenzie makes 72% of her free throws. Design a simulation to estimate the probability that she makes at least 8 of 10 shots.

steps.t: Assign numbers to the outcomes so their proportions match the probabilities.

work.text: 72 of the 100 two-digit numbers give a 72% chance of a make. The ranges must not overlap.

steps.t: Say how many numbers to generate per trial and whether repeats are allowed.

work.text: Generate 10 numbers from 00 to 99 for each trial. Repeats are allowed because each shot is independent.

steps.t: Say what to count in each trial.

work.text: Count how many of the 10 numbers are from 00 to 71.
At least 8 makes means eight, nine, or ten.

steps.t: Repeat for many trials, then estimate the probability.

work.text: Five trials with one success is only 20%. That is far too few to estimate the probability well.

questions.answer: Let 00 to 71 be a make and 72 to 99 a miss. Generate 10 numbers from 00 to 99 with repeats allowed. Count the numbers from 00 to 71. A trial is a success if there are at least 8. Repeat for many trials and divide the number of successes by the number of trials.

traps.title: Stopping after a few trials
traps.weak: In five trials we got 1 success, so the probability is 20%.
traps.better: Five trials is far too few. The estimate is the proportion of successes over a large number of trials, and it gets closer to the true probability as trials increase.

traps.title: Incomplete simulation design
traps.weak: Use a random number generator to simulate the free throws.
traps.better: Let 00 to 71 be a make and 72 to 99 a miss. Generate 10 numbers per trial with repeats allowed. Count the makes. A trial is a success if there are 8 or more makes. Run many trials and divide the number of successes by the number of trials.

traps.title: Repeats allowed when choosing stores
traps.weak: Generate 8 numbers from 1 to 800, repeats allowed.
traps.better: Generate 8 different numbers from 1 to 800, ignoring repeats, because a store cannot be chosen twice.

traps.title: Numbers that do not match the probability
traps.weak: Use 1 to 72 for a make and 1 to 28 for a miss.
traps.better: The numbers must not overlap. Use 01 to 72 for a make and 73 to 100 for a miss, so that 72% of the numbers represent a make.

traps.title: Probability from a short run
traps.weak: A fair coin must give exactly 50 heads in 100 tosses.
traps.better: The probability 0.5 describes the long-run relative frequency. A hundred tosses will usually be close to 50 heads but need not give exactly 50.

questions.stem: A spinner lands on blue with probability 0.30. Which assignment of digits 0 to 9 correctly simulates one spin?
opts: 0, 1, 2 are blue; 3 to 9 are not blue
0, 1, 2, 3 are blue; 4 to 9 are not blue
1 to 3 are blue; 3 to 9 are not blue
why: Correct. Three of ten digits give a probability of 0.30.
The digit 3 appears in both groups, so the assignment overlaps.

questions.stem: A simulation estimates the probability of at least two sixes in four dice rolls. After 20 trials the estimate is 0.10. Which action would most improve the estimate?
opts: Use a different random number table
why: The table does not fix a small sample of trials.
Correct. By the law of large numbers, more trials bring the relative frequency closer to the true probability.
Success is already defined by the problem.
Repeats are correct for die rolls, which are independent.

questions.stem: A club of 30 members has 12 seniors. A simulation picks 4 members at random for a committee and counts seniors. Which design is correct?
opts: Digits 0 to 9 are seniors; generate 4 numbers
Digits 01 to 12 are seniors; generate 4 numbers from 01 to 30 with repeats allowed
Digits 01 to 12 are seniors; generate 4 different numbers from 01 to 30
Digits 1 to 4 are seniors; generate 12 numbers
why: Repeats must not be allowed because a member cannot serve twice.
Correct. Twelve of 30 numbers are seniors and the 4 numbers must be different.
The numbers do not match the 12 seniors in 30 members.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the probability of an event?
opts: Whether the event is likely to happen next
The number of outcomes in the event
The proportion of times it occurs in the first 10 trials
The long-run relative frequency of the event over many trials
why: Probability does not predict a single next outcome.
A count of outcomes alone does not give a probability.
A short run can differ a lot from the true probability.
Correct. Probability is the relative frequency over a large number of trials.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A basketball player makes 65% of her free throws. The coach wants to estimate the probability that she makes at least 5 of 6 consecutive free throws.
parts: (a) Describe how to use two-digit random numbers 00 to 99 to simulate one trial.
(b) State what counts as a successful trial.
(c) In 200 trials, 62 were successes. Estimate the probability and state whether this estimate is exact.
(d) A teammate estimates from 8 trials. Explain why 200 trials is better.
sample: (a) Let 00 to 64 represent a make (65 numbers) and 65 to 99 a miss. Generate 6 numbers per trial, with repeats allowed because the shots are independent. Count the numbers in 00 to 64.
(b) A trial is a success if at least 5 of the 6 numbers are from 00 to 64.
(c) $62/200=0.31$. This is an estimate based on the trials, not the exact probability.
(d) By the law of large numbers, the relative frequency over more trials is closer to the true probability, so 200 trials gives a more reliable estimate than 8.
checklist: (a) 65 of 100 numbers assigned to a make
(b) Success defined as at least 5 makes
(d) Cites more trials or the law of large numbers

flags.text: The video mixes "repeats" and "duplicates" and uses 0 to 99 and 1 to 100 interchangeably. The page keeps both numbering systems but requires non-overlapping ranges.
Captions garble the video demo results; the stated simulated counts (2 of 7, 1 of 5) are used only as illustrations of small-trial estimates.
Exact values computed in code: P(3+ heads of 5)=0.500; P(8 US stores of 8)=0.0228; P(8+ makes of 10 at 0.72)=0.438; P(5+ of 6 at 0.65)=0.319.

Procedure section rewritten as three worked questions, one per example in the video. The questions describe the design only; the video's small demonstration results are mentioned in the step notes as warnings about too few trials.
